title: Three Matching Remainders
statement: How many ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ of integers with $0 \le x \le 34$, $0 \le y \le 34$ and $0 \le z \le 34$ satisfy both $xy + 6z \equiv yz + 6x \pmod{35}$ and $yz + 6x \equiv zx + 6y \pmod{35}$?
hints: Subtract the three expressions $xy + 6z$, $yz + 6x$ and $zx + 6y$ from one another in pairs. Each difference factorises into a product of two simple linear terms.

The differences are $(y-6)(x-z)$, $(z-6)(y-x)$ and $(x-6)(z-y)$. Modulo $35$, a product can vanish without either factor vanishing, so use the Chinese remainder theorem to work modulo $5$ and modulo $7$ separately.

Modulo a prime $p$, each product vanishes only if one of its factors does. Either $x, y, z$ are all equal, or exactly two of them equal $6$ and the third is a different residue. This gives $p + 3(p-1) = 4p - 3$ triples modulo $p$. It remains to combine the counts for $p = 5$ and $p = 7$.
solution: Subtracting the expressions in pairs and factorising gives $$(xy + 6z) - (yz + 6x) = (y-6)(x-z),$$ $$(yz + 6x) - (zx + 6y) = (z-6)(y-x),$$ $$(zx + 6y) - (xy + 6z) = (x-6)(z-y).$$ The two given congruences say that the first two products are $0$ modulo $35$. The third product is then also $0$, since the three products sum to $0$. So the system is equivalent to all three products being $0$ modulo $35$. Since $5$ and $7$ are coprime, an integer is divisible by $35$ exactly when it is divisible by both $5$ and $7$. So a triple satisfies the system modulo $35$ exactly when it satisfies the system modulo $5$ and modulo $7$. By the Chinese remainder theorem, each coordinate in $\{0, 1, \dots, 34\}$ corresponds to exactly one pair of residues modulo $5$ and modulo $7$. Hence triples modulo $35$ correspond one-to-one with pairs consisting of a triple modulo $5$ and a triple modulo $7$. The required count is therefore the product of the number of solutions modulo $5$ and the number modulo $7$. Now let $p$ be $5$ or $7$ and count triples of residues modulo $p$ satisfying the system. Because $p$ is prime, a product is $0$ modulo $p$ only if one of its factors is $0$. Case 1: $x \equiv y \equiv z$. All three differences vanish, so every such triple is a solution. There are $p$ of these. Case 2: $x, y, z$ are not all equal. Then at least two of the differences $x-z$, $y-x$, $z-y$ are nonzero, because if two of them were zero then the third would be too. Each nonzero difference forces the other factor in its product to vanish, so at least two of $y-6$, $z-6$, $x-6$ are $0$. Thus at least two of $x, y, z$ are congruent to $6$. Since they are not all equal, exactly two are congruent to $6$ and the third is not. Conversely, take any triple in which exactly two coordinates are $6$. Each product has the form (one variable $- 6$) times (difference of the other two). If that one variable is $6$, the first factor is $0$. If it is the odd variable, the other two are both $6$, so the difference is $0$. So all such triples are solutions. There are $3$ choices for the odd position and $p-1$ choices for its value, giving $3(p-1)$ triples. The two cases are disjoint, so there are $p + 3(p-1) = 4p - 3$ solutions modulo $p$. This is $17$ for $p = 5$ and $25$ for $p = 7$. The number of triples is $17 \cdot 25 = 425$. The answer is $425$. Why this works. crt, modular-arithmetic, casework: zero products modulo $35$ are hard to read directly because $35$ is composite, but splitting into its prime factors lets each product force a factor to vanish, leaving a short case split.
